purpose: This medication is used to treat several conditions where your immune system is overactive and causing inflammation, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and plaque psoriasis. It helps reduce pain, swelling, and other symptoms caused by these conditions. It can also slow down joint damage in certain types of arthritis.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called TNF (tumor necrosis factor) that causes inflammation. When your body makes too much TNF, it can attack healthy tissues and cause pain and damage. Adalimumab-aqvh works by attaching to that TNF protein and blocking it, which helps calm down the inflammation and protect your joints and tissues.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include redness, itching, or bruising at the injection site, upper respiratory infections like colds, headache, rash, and nausea. Some people may also notice mild stomach pain or back pain.
warnings: This medication lowers your immune system, which means you can get serious infections more easily — including bacterial, viral, fungal, and tuberculosis (TB) infections. You should be tested for TB before starting this medicine. Do not use it if you have an active infection. It may also increase the risk of certain cancers, including lymphoma. Tell your doctor right away if you notice signs of infection (fever, chills, cough), unusual lumps, or any new or worsening symptoms. Avoid live vaccines while taking this medication.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection). The dose and how often you take it depends on your condition — for example, for rheumatoid arthritis, a common dose is 40 mg every other week. Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to take and when. It comes in a prefilled pen or syringe that you can use at home after being trained by your healthcare provider.
